evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》 (天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692)
evidence.field: PDF p. 87; printed p. 75; headword 口 and entry prose, verified against attached scan pixels
evidence.text: The scanned entry identifies 口 as a pictograph shaped like a human mouth and gives ‘mouth’ as its basic meaning. It cites an oracle-bone use, 詩·豳風·鴟鴞 using 口 in the mouth sense, and bronze use as a clan sign. It also proposes that ancient forms were generally written in two strokes, with three-stroke forms possibly appearing by Han times; this stroke-history claim is the book's account, not independently confirmed here. I visually checked the headword, forms, prose and entry ending on the attached PDF p. 87 scan. PDF p. 88 begins with a continuation for 噲, not 口.
evidence.title: 字源 (2012 scan; edition details supplied and checked against project bibliography)

evidence.text: The institutional record groups 口 examples under oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and small-seal traditions, and identifies 口 as depicting a human mouth with upper and lower lips, used for eating and speaking. Its labels support the broad script-tradition sequence, but do not establish a detailed stroke-by-stroke development.
evidence.title: 漢字「口」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 甲骨部件分析 / entries 口 and 亼
evidence.text: The entry describes 口 as a frontal open-mouth form, with speaking and eating as bodily functions; it cites the oracle-bone use 合集13642 疾口 for mouth illness, and bronze uses as a clan name and 曰 ‘say’. It distinguishes 亼, a downward-facing or inverted-mouth component, from frontal 口. This warns against assigning eating-related component functions automatically wherever a graph looks mouth-like.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Ministry of Education, Taiwan
evidence.text: The entry reproduces the received Shuowen account 人所以言食也。象形。凡口之屬皆从口 and lists meanings including bodily mouth, an object's opening, a passage, a barrier, blade edge, break, and person-counting classifier. It cites 王充《論衡·道虛》 for an object's opening. These definitions and citations do not establish the first occurrence or a chronological semantic chain among the senses.
evidence.title: [A00480] 口 - 教育部《異體字字典》

gaps: The exact first attestation of graph 口 is not established; the cited oracle-bone examples are indexed examples, not a verified first occurrence.
The cited sources document the mouth sense and examples of opening and household-count uses, but do not date the beginning of each extended sense or establish a semantic path among them.
The 字源 proposal that ancient 口 forms were generally two strokes and three-stroke writing may appear by Han times has not been independently checked against source inscriptions.

The official character-specific Unicode Unihan page for U+53E3 could not be accessed. The local tracked kMandarin row was verified, but current reading metadata is not click-through corroborated here.
